source_text:
Λέγει μοι: Οἴδατε, φησίν, ὅτι ἐπὶ ξένης κατοικεῖτε ὑμεῖς οἱ δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ: ἡ γὰρ πόλις ὑμῶν μακράν ἐστιν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης: εἰ οὖν οἴδατε, φησί, τὴν πόλιν ὑμῶν, ἐν ᾗ μέλλετε κατοικεῖν, τί ὧδε ὑμεῖς ἑτοιμάζετε ἀγροὺς καὶ παρατάξεις πολυτελεῖς καὶ οἰκοδομὰς καὶ οἰκήματα μάταια;
ταῦτα οὖν ὁ ἑτοιμάζων εἰς ταύτην τὴν πόλιν οὐ δύναται ἐπανακάμψαι εἰς τὴν ἰδίαν πόλιν.
ἄφρον καὶ δίψυχε καὶ ταλαίπωρε ἄνθρωπε, οὐ νοεῖς, ὅτι ταῦτα πάντα ἀλλότριά εἰσι καὶ ὑπ’ ἐξουσίαν ἑτέρου εἰσίν; ἐρεῖ γὰρ ὁ κύριος τῆς πόλεως ταύτης: Οὐ θέλω σε κατοικεῖν εἰς τὴν πόλιν μου, ἀλλ’ ἔξελθε ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης, ὅτι τοῖς νόμοις μου οὐ χρᾶσαι.
σὺ οὖν ἔχων ἀγροὺς καὶ οἰκήσεις καὶ ἑτέρας ὑπάρξεις πολλάς, ἐκβαλλόμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τί ποιήσεις σου τὸν ἀγρὸν καὶ τὴν οἰκίαν καὶ τὰ λοιπά, ὅσα ἡτοίμασας σεαυτῷ; λέγει γάρ σοι δικαίως ὁ κύριος τῆς χώρας ταύτης: Ἢ τοῖς νόμοις μου χρῶ ἢ ἐκχώρει ἐκ τῆς χώρας μου.
σὺ οὖν τί μέλλεις ποιεῖν, ἔχων νόμον ἐν τῇ σῇ πόλει; ἕνεκεν τῶν ἀγρῶν σου καὶ τῆς λοιπῆς ὑπάρξεως τὸν νόμον σου πάντως ἀπαρνήσῃ καὶ πορεύσῃ τῷ νόμῳ τῆς πόλεως ταύτης; βλέπε, μὴ ἀσύμφορόν ἐστιν ἀπαρνῆσαι τὸν νόμον σου: ἐὰν γὰρ ἐπανακάμψαι θελήσῃς εἰς τὴν πόλιν σου, οὐ μὴ παραδεχθήσῃ, ὅτι ἀπηρνήσω τὸν νόμον τῆς πόλεώς σου, καὶ ἐκκλεισθήσῃ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς.
βλέπε οὖν σύ: ὡς ἐπὶ ξένης κατοικῶν μηδὲν πλέον ἑτοίμαζε σεαυτῷ εἰ μὴ τὴν αὐτάρκειαν τὴν ἀρκετήν σοι, καὶ ἕτοιμος γίνου, ἵνα, ὅταν θέλῃ ὁ δεσπότης τῆς πόλεως ταύτης ἐκβαλεῖν σε ἀντιταξάμενον τῷ νόμῳ αὐτοῦ, ἐξέλθῃς ἐκ τῆς πόλεως αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπέλθῃς ἐν τῇ πόλει σου καὶ τῷ σῷ νόμῳ χρήσῃ ἀνυβρίστως ἀγαλλιώμενος.
βλέπετε οὖν ὑμεῖς οἱ δουλεύοντες τῷ κυρίῳ καὶ ἔχοντες αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν καρδίαν: ἐργάζεσθε τὰ ἔργα τοῦ θεοῦ μνημονεύοντες τῶν ἐντολῶν αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν ὧν ἐπηγγείλατο, καὶ πιστεύσατε αὐτῷ, ὅτι ποιήσει αὐτάς, ἐὰν αἱ ἐντολαὶ αὐτοῦ φυλαχθῶσιν.
ἀντὶ ἀγρῶν οὖν ἀγοράζετε ψυχὰς θλιβομένας, καθά τις δυνατός ἐστι, καὶ χήρας καὶ ὀρφανοὺς ἐπισκέπτεσθε καὶ μὴ παραβλέπετε αὐτούς, καὶ τὸν πλοῦτον ὑμῶν καὶ τὰς παρατάξεις πάσας εἰς τοιούτους ἀγροὺς καὶ οἰκίας δαπανᾶτε, ἃς ἐλάβετε παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ.
εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπλούτισεν ὑμᾶς ὁ δεσπότης, ἵνα ταύτας τὰς διακονίας τελέσητε αὐτῷ: πολὺ βέλτιόν ἐστι τοιούτους ἀγροὺς ἀγοράζειν καὶ κτήματα καὶ οἴκους, οὓς εὑρήσεις ἐν τῇ πόλει σου, ὅταν ἐπιδημήσῃς εἰς αὐτήν.
αὕτη ἡ πολυτέλεια καλὴ καὶ ἱερά, λύπην μὴ ἔχουσα μηδὲ φόβον, ἔχουσα δὲ χαράν. τὴν οὖν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἐθνῶν μὴ πράσσετε: ἀσύμφορον γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῖν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ.
τὴν δὲ ἰδίαν πολυτέλειαν πράσσετε, ἐν ᾗ δύνασθε χαρῆναι, καὶ μὴ παραχαράσσετε μηδὲ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου ἅψησθε μηδὲ ἐπιθυμεῖτε αὐτοῦ: πονηρὸν γάρ ἐστιν ἀλλοτρίων ἐπιθυμεῖν. τὸ δὲ σὸν ἔργον ἐργάζου, καὶ σωθήσῃ.
thought_title: Citizens of a far city must not invest in this foreign land
orientation: The commandments are finished, and the Shepherd now begins a series of parables. In this first one he tells the servants of God that they live in a foreign city and should not sink their wealth into it.
pass_a_gloss: He says to me: You know, he says, that you dwell in a foreign land, you the servants of God; for your city is far from this city. If therefore you know, he says, your city, in which you are about to dwell, why do you here prepare fields and costly displays and buildings and vain dwellings? Therefore the one who prepares these things for this city is not able to return to his own city. Foolish and double-minded and wretched man, do you not understand that all these things are foreign and are under the authority of another? For the lord of this city will say: I do not want you to dwell in my city, but go out from this city, because you do not use my laws. You therefore, having fields and dwellings and many other possessions, when you are cast out by him, what will you do with your field and your house and the rest, as much as you prepared for yourself? For the lord of this country says to you justly: Either use my laws or depart from my country. You therefore, what are you about to do, having a law in your own city? For the sake of your fields and the rest of your possession will you entirely deny your law and walk by the law of this city? See that it is not unprofitable to deny your law; for if you wish to return to your city, you will certainly not be received, because you denied the law of your city, and you will be shut out from it. See therefore you: as one dwelling in a foreign land, prepare nothing more for yourself except the self-sufficiency that is sufficient for you, and be ready, so that, when the master of this city wishes to cast you out for opposing his law, you may go out from his city and depart into your city and use your own law, rejoicing without insult. See therefore you who serve the Lord and have him in your heart: work the works of God, remembering his commandments and the promises which he promised, and trust him, that he will do them, if his commandments are kept. Therefore instead of fields buy afflicted souls, as each one is able, and visit widows and orphans and do not overlook them, and spend your wealth and all your displays on such fields and houses, which you received from God. For to this end the master enriched you, that you may complete these ministries for him; it is much better to buy such fields and possessions and houses, which you will find in your city, when you arrive in it. This luxury is good and holy, having no grief nor fear, but having joy. Therefore do not practice the luxury of the nations; for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God. But practice your own luxury, in which you are able to rejoice, and do not counterfeit nor touch what is another's nor desire it; for it is evil to desire what belongs to others. But work your own work, and you will be saved.

lemmas.gloss: to arrive, to be at home

choices.why: παράταξις here means ostentatious arrangements or shows of wealth, not military formations; 'displays' captures the sense of visible luxury being condemned
οἴκημα is a dwelling or habitation, and μάταιος means vain or empty; the phrase contrasts with the true city
ἀσύμφορος means not advantageous or not beneficial; 'unprofitable' keeps the economic metaphor of the passage
ἀνυβρίστως means without being insulted or mistreated; the rejoicing is free from the abuse of the foreign city's master
παραχαράσσω means to falsify or debase, especially coinage; in context it means not imitating the luxury of the nations with false substitutes
πολυτέλεια means extravagance or costly display; 'luxury' captures the moral condemnation, and 'the nations' is the standard rendering of τὰ ἔθνη for non-believers
rejected: the costly display of the heathen

pass_b_english: The Shepherd said to me, “You know that you, the servants of God, are living in a foreign land. For your own city is far from this city. If, then, you know your own city, the one where you are going to live, why do you prepare fields here, and costly furnishings, and buildings, and vain dwellings? Whoever prepares these things for this city cannot return to his own city.

“Foolish, double-minded, wretched man! Do you not grasp that all these things belong to another, and are under another’s authority? For the lord of this city will say, ‘I do not want you living in my city. Leave this city, for you do not live by my laws.’

“You have fields and dwellings and many other possessions. When he casts you out, what will you do with your field and your house and everything else that you have prepared for yourself? For the lord of this country justly says to you, ‘Either live by my laws, or leave my country.’

“What, then, are you going to do, you who have a law in your own city? For the sake of your fields and the rest of your possessions, will you deny your law altogether, and walk by the law of this city? Take care. It may prove unprofitable to deny your law. For if you wish to return to your own city, you will certainly not be received, because you denied the law of your city. You will be shut out of it.

“So take care. As one who lives in a foreign land, prepare nothing more for yourself than what is enough for your needs, and be ready. Then, when the master of this city wishes to cast you out for opposing his law, you can leave his city and go away to your own city. There you can live by your own law, rejoicing and free from insult.

“So take care, you who serve the Lord and have him in your heart. Do the works of God, remembering his commandments and the promises he made. Believe him, that he will keep his promises if his commandments are kept.

“So instead of fields, buy afflicted souls, each of you as he is able. Visit widows and orphans, and do not overlook them. Spend your wealth and all your furnishings, which you received from God, on fields and houses of this kind.

“For this is why the Master made you rich: so that you might carry out these ministries for him. It is far better to buy fields and possessions and houses of this kind, which you will find in your own city when you come home to it.
“This extravagance is good and sacred. It has no grief and no fear, but it has joy. So do not practice the extravagance of the nations, for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God.

“Practice your own extravagance, in which you can rejoice. Do not counterfeit. Do not touch what belongs to another, and do not desire it, for it is evil to desire what belongs to others. Do your own work, and you will be saved.”

problems.fix: Footnote: metaphorical language for caring for needy

fixed: Glossary issue: 'double-mindedness' is not a mistranslation; the English uses 'double-minded' consistently for the concept, and the glossary already lists the term. No edit needed.
Mistranslation: 'buy afflicted souls' is a literal rendering of ἀγοράζετε ψυχὰς θλιβομένας, but 'redeem' better conveys the charitable sense of the metaphor. Changed to 'redeem afflicted souls'.

problems.why: Unclear what this refers to; likely 'luxurious furnishings' or 'ostentatious decorations'.

fixed: Changed 'costly displays' to 'luxurious displays' to better reflect the sense of 'παρατάξεις πολυτελεῖς' as ostentatious or luxurious displays.

problems.why: In context of luxury and possessions, 'counterfeit' is odd; Greek kibdēleuō may mean 'adulterate' or 'deal falsely,' not make fake money.
problems.fix: Translate as 'do not deal falsely' or 'do not adulterate' to match context of honest dealings.

fixed: Changed 'do not counterfeit' to 'do not deal falsely' to match the context of honest dealings with possessions; the Greek μὴ παραχαράσσετε means 'do not falsify/deal falsely,' not specifically 'make counterfeit money.'
